summary:
TerraPulse is an open, browser-based Earth observatory that turns synthetic aperture radar (SAR) into evidence anyone can explore. Users choose a place or drop in their own GeoTIFF, GeoJSON or CSV files. TerraPulse recognises each layer and flies a 3D globe to the location. It then lays Sentinel-1 radar change, Sentinel-2 imagery, Copernicus elevation and OpenStreetMap data over an interactive 3D terrain, and can record a narrated story video.

For the Dancing with the SARs challenge, we focused on what radar uniquely offers: it sees through cloud and darkness, when optical satellites fail. Our showcase is the August 2024 Thame glacial lake outburst in Nepal. There, radar backscatter brightens on the drained lake, and a simplified flood model, timed to published simulations, shows the surge reaching Thame. That model places 62 of the 189 nearby mapped buildings in its path. A one-command pipeline rebuilds the same analysis for any region from free open data, as shown for the Valencia floods of 2024.

It matters because disaster evidence is often locked in specialist tools. TerraPulse makes it visible and honest: every layer is labelled as observed, derived or modelled.
details:
What it does and how it works

TerraPulse is a browser-based Earth observatory for surface change. You start in a spacecraft cockpit, the team’s own artwork. The Earth turns in the window, and four pillars open the views: 2D Map, 3D Terrain, Evidence Tables and ML Models.

You can choose a showcase place or drop in your own GeoTIFF, GeoJSON, CSV or Excel files. TerraPulse inspects each file and works out what it is: an elevation model, radar, optical imagery, a water mask or a table. It then suggests suitable analyses and flies the globe to the data’s location.

The analyses include:

  • Sentinel-1 radar backscatter change, as a before/after log-ratio in dB;
  • water masks from Sentinel-2 (NDWI);
  • slope and hillshade from the elevation model;
  • a simplified flood path model.

The results are draped over an interactive 3D terrain. A scripted story turns them into a narrated video that the browser records directly.

A one-command pipeline builds a complete workspace for any area of up to 1° × 1° from free open data, with no accounts needed. It gathers Copernicus elevation, the clearest Sentinel-2 before/after images, a matched Sentinel-1 radar pair and its change map, and OpenStreetMap buildings.

Showcases

  • Thame glacial lake outburst, Nepal (August 2024): radar brightening on the drained lake, and a flood model timed to published simulations that places 62 of 189 nearby mapped buildings in the flood path.
  • Valencia floods, Spain (October 2024): built automatically by the pipeline.

Benefits

  • No accounts or installs: it runs in a browser on free open data.
  • Works anywhere: it isn’t tied to one place; any region can be built or uploaded.
  • Sees through cloud: radar shows change when optical satellites are blocked by cloud or darkness.
  • Labelled honestly: every layer carries a badge (satellite, observed, derived, model, synthetic or illustrative), so evidence is never confused with simulation.
  • Recordable: stories export as video for briefings and outreach.

Intended impact

We want to make SAR evidence understandable to people who aren’t remote-sensing specialists: local responders, journalists, students and community planners. After a disaster, they should be able to see what changed, where water went and what it reached, quickly and honestly, in any region.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python, GLSL shaders.
  • Frontend: React and Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber (3D terrain, flood shader, debris particles, globe), MapLibre GL (2D maps), geotiff.js (in-browser raster reading), proj4.
  • Backend (optional): FastAPI, pandas, and scikit-learn for a guided Random Forest with checks against data leakage.
  • Data pipeline: Node.js scripts using STAC catalogues and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF range reads; Python with OpenCV and SciPy for the artwork cutouts.
  • Data: Sentinel-1 RTC (Microsoft Planetary Computer), Sentinel-2 L2A (Earth Search), Copernicus DEM GLO-30, OpenStreetMap, NASA GIBS Blue and Black Marble.
  • Hosting: Vercel for the web app; Docker for the optional API.
  • Hardware: standard laptops; 3D rendering runs on ordinary integrated graphics.

Creativity

  • The interface is the team’s own painting, made interactive. The real pillars were cut out of the artwork and serve as the navigation, with carved, glowing inscriptions.
  • Entering data turns the globe and dives into the place it describes.
  • Analysis becomes storytelling: the flood front advances on a clock, debris flows down the valley, and buildings change colour as the modelled flood reaches them, all exportable as video.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific integrity:
    • No invented data. Event facts come from the published study (NHESS 2026).
    • Inferences, such as which lakes drained, are labelled “inferred”.
    • The flood model is clearly marked as simplified.
    • The debris particles are marked as illustrative.
    • NISAR is noted as launching after the event, so it isn’t used as evidence for it.
  • Accessibility and reach: free data only, works without the Python API, adapts to desktop and tablet screens, and respects reduced-motion settings.
  • Limits of radar: we use backscatter change, not InSAR ground displacement, and say so. Rice fields and frozen lakes can be misread, so we flag those caveats.
  • Licensing and credit: Copernicus, OpenStreetMap, NASA and Esri attribution is shown in the app, the videos and the README.
